cards.question: Which 1987 report, also known as the Brundtland report, defined sustainable development?
cards.answer: The World Commission on Environment and Development's report 'Our Common Future'.
distractors: The Stockholm Declaration on the Human Environment
The Rio Declaration on Environment and Development
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights

cards.question: What is the Brundtland definition of sustainable development?
cards.answer: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
distractors: Development that maximises economic growth while limiting emissions to a fixed annual cap
Development that protects every ecosystem from any human influence
Development that guarantees equal income to all present generations

cards.question: Which three dimensions must all be fulfilled to achieve sustainability?
cards.answer: Society, environment and economy.
distractors: Energy, materials and waste
Technology, policy and finance
Production, consumption and disposal

cards.question: In the three-pillar model, what does the overlap of society and economy represent?
cards.answer: Equitable.
distractors: Bearable
Viable
Sustainable

cards.question: In the three-pillar model, what does the overlap of society and environment represent?
cards.answer: Bearable.
distractors: Equitable
Viable
Sustainable

cards.question: In the three-pillar model, what does the overlap of environment and economy represent?
cards.answer: Viable.
distractors: Equitable
Bearable
Sustainable

cards.question: In the three-pillar model, where does 'sustainable' sit?
cards.answer: At the centre where society, environment and economy all overlap.
distractors: In the overlap of only society and economy
In the overlap of only environment and economy
In the environment circle alone

cards.question: Which pillar is described as Earth's life support system, and which as human societies and economies?
cards.answer: Environment is Earth's life support system; society and economy are the human systems that depend on it.
distractors: Economy is Earth's life support system; society and environment are human systems
Society is Earth's life support system; economy and environment are human systems
All three pillars are described as human systems

cards.question: Why must sustainability assessment consider all three dimensions rather than only the environment?
cards.answer: Because sustainability is achieved only when the social, economic and environmental dimensions are all fulfilled together.
distractors: Because the environmental dimension is legally irrelevant to engineers
Because economic and social dimensions can substitute for a poor environmental result
Because assessing one dimension automatically covers the others

cards.question: What is the key message about human activities and the environment in the 'What is sustainability?' introduction?
cards.answer: The environment is challenged by human activities, so we need to reduce our environmental impact to stay within the planetary boundaries.
distractors: The environment is unaffected by human activities at current scales
Environmental impacts are only a local problem with no global consequences
Economic growth alone will restore planetary boundaries

cards.question: What is the Stockholm Declaration of 1972 described as in the origin of today's SDGs?
cards.answer: Consensus I: our activities, particularly industrialisation, are impacting the global environment, so we need to assess and manage that impact.
distractors: Consensus II: a reconciliation of environment with economic development and human rights
A declaration that human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights
A report that defined sustainable development for future generations

cards.question: What did the 1992 Rio Declaration aim to reconcile?
cards.answer: The Stockholm Declaration (environment) with economic development and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
distractors: The Brundtland report with the EU Taxonomy
The Paris Agreement with the Green Deal
The Stockholm Declaration with the SDG progress reports

cards.question: From which two interacting forces did the modern sustainability concept emerge?
cards.answer: Economic development and environmentalism.
distractors: Industrial policy and consumer demand
Human rights and military security only
Technology and population growth

cards.question: According to the Rio Declaration, who is at the centre of concerns for sustainable development?
cards.answer: Human beings.
distractors: Ecosystems
Economies
Future technologies

cards.question: According to the Rio Declaration, what role should environmental protection have in the development process?
cards.answer: It shall constitute an integral part of the development process.
distractors: It shall be pursued only after development goals are met
It shall be a voluntary add-on to development
It shall replace development in vulnerable regions

cards.question: According to the Rio Declaration, whose developmental and environmental needs should be met equitably?
cards.answer: Those of present and future generations.
distractors: Those of the present generation only
Those of developed countries only
Those of ecosystems only

cards.question: What are the two reasons given for why the Rio consensus was needed (beyond reconciling Stockholm with development)?
cards.answer: It was needed for global security and to adhere to Universal Human Rights.
distractors: It was needed for trade liberalisation and carbon pricing
It was needed for biodiversity targets and resource scarcity quotas
It was needed for corporate reporting and taxation

cards.question: In which year was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted, and why does it matter for sustainability obligations?
cards.answer: 1948; it is one of the foundations that Rio reconciled with environmental protection and development.
distractors: 1972; it started the call to assess the impacts of industrialisation
1987; it defined sustainable development
1992; it defined the three pillars

cards.question: What does Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights state?
cards.answer: All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.
distractors: Everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for health and well-being
Everyone is entitled to all rights and freedoms without distinction of any kind
Everyone has the right to a clean and healthy environment

cards.question: What does Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights state?
cards.answer: Everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in the Declaration, without distinction of any kind.
distractors: All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights
Everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for health and well-being
Everyone has the right to work and to equal pay

cards.question: What does Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights state?
cards.answer: Everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for the health and well-being of himself and of his family.
distractors: All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights
Everyone is entitled to all rights and freedoms without distinction of any kind
Everyone has the right to participate in decisions on resource use

cards.question: What is the difference between the Stockholm Declaration (1972) and the Rio Declaration (1992) in terms of focus?
cards.answer: Stockholm focused on assessing and managing human impact on the global environment; Rio reconciled this with economic development and human rights.
distractors: Stockholm defined the SDGs; Rio defined the planetary boundaries
Stockholm focused on human rights; Rio focused on the EU Taxonomy
Stockholm reconciled environment with development; Rio focused on industrial impacts

cards.question: What is the central economic claim of the European Green Deal as shown in the lecture?
cards.answer: Economic growth is decoupled from greenhouse gas emissions.
distractors: Economic growth must be reduced to cut emissions
Emissions grow proportionally to economic growth
Greenhouse gas emissions are offset entirely by taxation

cards.question: What is the purpose of the EU Taxonomy?
cards.answer: To define environmentally sustainable economic activities.
distractors: To set carbon prices for all EU industries
To rank countries by SDG progress
To list banned chemicals in the EU

cards.question: What is the EU Taxonomy intended to incentivise?
cards.answer: Transitions to 'sustainable' activities and investments.
distractors: Reduction of imports from outside the EU
Increased consumption of renewable materials only
Compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights

cards.question: In 'From commitments to regulations', what do the overlapping areas of the three-pillar model map to?
cards.answer: Permissible activities and value creation.
distractors: Carbon budgets and planetary boundaries
Equitable and bearable only
Taxation and subsidies

cards.question: How does the lecture connect global commitments to engineering practice?
cards.answer: Commitments such as the declarations become regulations (e.g. the EU Taxonomy) that define which activities are permissible and where value is created.
distractors: Commitments are only symbolic and do not affect practice
Commitments apply to governments only and never to engineering design
Commitments replace the need for quantitative assessment

cards.question: Which organisation's report is cited for progress towards the SDGs in the introductory video?
cards.answer: The United Nations (UN SDG Report 2025).
distractors: The International Energy Agency
The European Commission
The Stockholm Resilience Centre

cards.question: What does the planetary boundaries framework (Richardson et al., 2023) address?
cards.answer: Limits for Earth system processes that humanity should stay within to avoid risking the planet.
distractors: National emission targets set by the EU
A list of SDG indicators for each country
Economic limits for corporate growth

cards.question: Why does the introductory video show PCB concentrations in Arctic animals?
cards.answer: To illustrate pollution: persistent chemicals accumulate in top predators to levels at which effects (e.g. reduced reproduction, immune effects) are seen.
distractors: To show that PCBs are no longer present in the Arctic
To illustrate resource scarcity of arctic fish
To show greenhouse gas uptake by marine mammals

cards.question: What effect threshold is shown for seals in the PCB figure?
cards.answer: Reduced reproduction at about 25,000 ng/g fat.
distractors: 50% survival of mink at 50 ng/g fat
Immune effects in rhesus monkeys at 1,000,000 ng/g fat
Memory effects in man at 500,000 ng/g fat

cards.question: In the PCB figure, what do LOAEL and NOAEL stand for?
cards.answer: Lowest observed adverse effect level and no observed adverse effect level.
distractors: Lowest observed acceptable emission level and no observed acceptable emission level
Limit of annual exposure level and norm of annual exposure level
Local organism adverse exposure limit and national organism adverse exposure limit

cards.question: What is the difference between LOAEL and NOAEL?
cards.answer: LOAEL is the lowest dose at which an adverse effect is observed; NOAEL is the highest dose at which no adverse effect is observed.
distractors: LOAEL applies to humans and NOAEL to animals
LOAEL is a legal limit and NOAEL is a measured value
LOAEL is the highest dose with no effect and NOAEL is the lowest dose with an effect

cards.question: What does the biodiversity slide in the introduction warn about?
cards.answer: Biodiversity is threatened by human activities.
distractors: Biodiversity is increasing due to protected areas
Biodiversity is only threatened in the Arctic
Biodiversity loss is already reversed

cards.question: What trend does the IEA (2019) figure show about key materials?
cards.answer: Growth in demand for key materials, e.g. for clean energy transitions.
distractors: A decline in demand for materials as clean energy grows
Constant demand for key materials
Falling material demand through efficiency alone

cards.question: What are the three learning outcomes of the 'What is sustainability?' video?
cards.answer: Explain the definition of sustainability, explain the three pillars, and explain that our planet is at risk environmentally and that we need to reduce our impacts.
distractors: Define LCA, compute a carbon footprint and perform a cost analysis
Explain the SDGs, planetary boundaries and circular economy
Explain EU law, the Taxonomy and carbon taxes

cards.question: What are the three key take-aways of the 'What is sustainability?' video?
cards.answer: Assessment should consider social, economic and environmental dimensions; the environment is challenged by human activities; we must reduce impact to stay within the planetary boundaries.
distractors: Only the environment needs quantitative assessment; economy is secondary; SDGs are legally binding
Growth must stop; technology cannot help; regulation is irrelevant
Only the economy matters; social aspects are optional; environment is stable

cards.question: Why use quantitative methods to assess sustainability?
cards.answer: 'You cannot manage what you cannot measure.'
distractors: Because qualitative methods are not permitted in sustainability work
Because quantitative results are always certain
Because the SDGs require numerical targets for each engineer

cards.question: Why does the course target all engineers?
cards.answer: Engineers have a special role to play in sustainability practices.
distractors: Only environmental engineers are responsible for sustainability
Sustainability is mainly an economic matter
Engineers are exempt from social responsibility

distractors: Because no single teacher is qualified
To reduce the workload of the main course responsible
To rotate who grades the exam

cards.answer: To provide a sustainability foundation for all engineers.

To teach regulatory law

distractors: Students must use every module for every case study
Students only need to pick one module
